title: Teen's Plant-Based Plastic Could Help Clean Up Microplastic Pollution
summary:
Microplastics are everywhere — in oceans, soil, food, and even the air we breathe. Because they're so tiny, removing them is incredibly difficult. But 18-year-old Arya Satheesh may have found a solution.

The Irish teen developed Eco Purge, a plant-based plastic that naturally decomposes while helping break down microplastics already in the environment. Her invention earned her the European regional title at The Earth Prize in May 2026, along with $12,500 in prize money and access to experts to help her develop the project further.

Arya first became interested in microplastics in 2024, when she created a water-quality sensor for a national science competition. Her device could detect microplastics in water, but it couldn't remove them. Determined to fix that, she began developing Eco Purge.

To make the bioplastic, she needed two natural enzymes. She contacted several biotechnology companies, but their samples were too expensive for a high school student. Undeterred, she reached out to Professor Kevin O'Connor, a researcher at BiOrbic in Ireland. He obtained the enzyme samples and helped her gain access to a laboratory at a local university.

By early 2026, Arya had her first prototype. She tested it by placing a set amount of microplastic with Eco Purge in soil, salt water, and fresh water. She observed the samples for six weeks. To her delight, at the end of the trial, both the microplastic and the Eco Purge had decomposed in each sample.

Arya still faces challenges before Eco Purge can be widely available. The enzymes only work on certain types of plastic, and high temperatures can damage them. Producing large amounts of enzymes could also be expensive. But she's determined to overcome these hurdles and keep improving Eco Purge.

"Science isn't just about understanding the world," she reflects. "It's about leaving it better than we found it."
why_it_matters: Microplastic pollution is a systemic problem created by how the world makes and throws away plastic, and clean-up technology lags far behind production. A cheap, plant-based material that both replaces plastic and helps break down existing waste would change the maths for governments and companies under pressure to cut pollution — though most school-lab prototypes never survive the jump to industrial scale.

background_read: Microplastics are plastic fragments smaller than five millimetres, created when bigger plastic items break apart or when tiny beads escape from cosmetics. Their size is the whole problem: they slip through most water treatment filters and end up in oceans, soil, rain and even the air we breathe.

Bioplastics are made from plants — corn starch or sugarcane, for example — instead of petroleum. Many are designed to break down faster than ordinary plastic, but most still need specific conditions, such as an industrial composter, to decompose properly.

Enzymes are proteins that work like tiny machines, speeding up chemical reactions. They are already used in laundry detergents and in experimental recycling that breaks PET bottles back into their basic building blocks.
The Earth Prize is an international competition that challenges students to design solutions to environmental problems; winners receive prize money and mentorship to develop their ideas further.
BiOrbic, where Professor Kevin O'Connor works, is an Irish research centre devoted to the bioeconomy — replacing oil-based materials and fuels with biological ones.

perspectives.description: Arya shows what happens when a student refuses to accept a dead end: her first device could only detect microplastics, so she built something that could attack them. Competitions like The Earth Prize matter because they attach money and expert help to teenage ideas that would otherwise stall.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the science is still small-scale
perspectives.description: A six-week test on small samples in a lab is not proof that Eco Purge works in a real river or landfill, where temperatures, chemicals and plastic types vary wildly. The enzymes only attack certain plastics and are costly to produce, so the gap between a promising prototype and a usable product is still huge.

Many bioplastics have looked promising in the lab and then struggled with cost, durability or waste systems that cannot handle them. Meanwhile, the amount of plastic entering the environment keeps growing, so clean-up inventions are running against a moving target.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what needs to happen next
perspectives.description: To scale up, Arya needs funding, lab partners and testing in real outdoor conditions, not just soil and water samples. Policy will also decide the outcome: if governments tax ordinary plastic or require compostable packaging, a product like Eco Purge becomes commercially viable much faster.
